name: Umar Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Umar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and what you say stays confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do roofs. Mostly new houses on estates, three-bedroom semis, that sort of thing, for a family builder I've been with sixteen years. Pete, the foreman, picks me up at half six because we live two streets apart, and we're on the scaffold by seven, setting out the trusses, which are the triangle frames that hold the roof up, then bracing, felt, battens, and the tilers come behind us. I take a flask of sweet tea and two cheese sandwiches, same every day, Samira says I'm the easiest man alive to feed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being up high on a clear morning, you can see the whole estate and the hills behind. And I like that a roof is right or it's wrong, there's no in between, the rain tells you. What gets to me is the weather, I've been soaked through more days than I can count, and the young ones who think a nail gun means you don't have to measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, and that's about it. I'm not one for big opinions. Pete would make some joke about it at tea break and we'd move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I never thought much of it anyway. I don't use these AI things, my son Yusuf set up my phone and I use it to ring people and look at the football scores. I'd be glad nothing changed, I like my job as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at all. Same firm, same roofs, keep putting money by every month like we do. We'd probably redo the bathroom next year, which we'd planned already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone at your firm tried to use AI for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss's daughter does the office now, and I think she uses it for the letters and the quotes. Fine by me, as long as the wages go in on Friday. I wouldn't know how it works and I don't need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want to change, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better vans, and an end to the rushing at the end of the month when the boss wants houses signed off. That's people, not machines. Machines don't rush you, the bank rushes the boss and the boss rushes us.

S0.say: I'd say there you go and leave it at that, because I'm not one for big opinions. Pete would joke about it at tea break and we'd move on.
S0.think: Privately he never thought much of AI, doesn't use it and only uses his phone for calls and football scores. He'd be glad nothing changed because he likes his job as it is.
S0.do: Carries on with the same firm on the same roofs and keeps putting money aside every month. Goes ahead with redoing the bathroom next year as already planned.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing much to feel.
S0.quote: Machines don't rush you, the bank rushes the boss and the boss rushes us.
S0.fieldNote: Umar is quiet and content, with a fixed routine and little interest in big opinions. He sees pressure at work as coming from money, not technology, but without blaming anyone in particular. AI is something the office uses, not him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's how it goes, things change. My dad's generation did roofs with no nail guns and no ready-made trusses, and we got used to those. I'd keep it short, I'm not going to make a song and dance about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think roofs go anywhere soon. Every roof has its little problem, a chimney, a valley, a wall that's two centimetres out, and you sort it with your eyes and hands. Maybe the trusses come even more ready-made, but somebody still has to be up there in the wind putting them together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mainly. If the firm brought in some new machine, I'd let the young ones learn it and I'd keep doing what I do. I'd wait and see, because I've heard about the end of roofing three times already and here I still am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little wary, but mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the young ones learn the machines. Would that worry you, being the one who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might, a bit, if the boss started treating them like they were worth more. But sixteen years counts for something with him, he's old-fashioned that way. And there's plenty of roofing work round here, every estate going up needs a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samira say about your plan to wait and see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd roll her eyes, she always says I'd wait and see if the house was on fire. But she knows we've got money put by, more than a year's worth, and the rent from the little house my brother and I bought. So she'd let me be stubborn, within reason.

S1.say: I'd say that's how it goes and things change, just as his dad's generation got used to nail guns and ready-made trusses. I'd keep it short and not make a big deal of it.
S1.think: Privately he doesn't think roofs go anywhere soon, because every roof has its own problem that you fix with your eyes and hands. Trusses might come more ready-made, but someone still has to assemble them up in the wind.
S1.do: Keeps working as normal and leaves any new machines for younger workers to learn. Waits to see what happens, trusting his sixteen years with the firm, plentiful local roofing work and his savings and rental income.
S1.feel: Calm, with a touch of wariness.
S1.quote: She always says I'd wait and see if the house was on fire.
S1.fieldNote: Umar's steadiness comes from experience: he's heard the end of roofing predicted before. His savings and the rental house with his brother let him be stubborn without much risk. He trusts his long loyalty to the firm to count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot on a roof in the rain. That's what I'd say at tea break, and I'd mean it. People have been promising me robots since I was an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But off the record, if it really happened, I'd be worried, of course. I'm forty-three, I've got a mortgage and two kids, and roofing is all I know. The money would keep us going a good while, but I'd be lying if I said I knew what I'd do after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd put the bathroom off and keep that money in the bank. I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and just build up the savings, and we'd skip the trip to see Samira's family this summer, which costs a lot with four flights. Then I'd keep working and wait to see if these robots really turn up, because I'm not giving up a good job over something on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I'd be quiet about it, but I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lose sleep over it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some nights, probably. I'd lie there thinking about Yusuf, he says he wants to do roofs with me when he leaves school, and I always liked the idea. I'd be thinking, what am I handing him, nothing?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd believe it when you see it, but you'd also start cutting back straight away. Do you believe it or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I suppose half of me doesn't believe it and the other half does the sums anyway. My dad always said, hope for the best, put money under the mattress for the worst. So I'd do both.

S2.say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot on a roof in the rain. People have been promising robots since I was an apprentice.
S2.think: Privately he'd be worried, at forty-three with a mortgage, two kids and roofing as the only work he knows. His savings would last a good while, but he doesn't know what he'd do after.
S2.do: Puts off the bathroom and keeps that money in the bank, stops extra mortgage payments and skips a costly family trip abroad. Keeps working and waits to see whether robots really arrive before giving up his job.
S2.feel: Quietly worried, with some sleepless nights over his son.
S2.quote: I'll believe it when I see a robot on a roof in the rain.
S2.fieldNote: Umar's public disbelief and private sums sit side by side, and he admitted it with good humour. The real sting is his son's wish to follow him into roofing. His savings give him a sense of control even as the fast picture unsettles him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing as before, I'd say I'll believe it when I see it. But I'd probably listen a bit more when the young ones talk about it at break. Five years is close enough that people would be talking about it on the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be forty-eight and Yusuf would be eighteen. That's the bit that gets me, because he'd be choosing his trade just as this lands. For me, with the money we have, I'd probably get through, but I wouldn't want him starting on the roofs then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, nothing changes for me there. I'd keep putting money away, a bit more than now. And I'd sit Yusuf down, maybe in a couple of years, and tell him to look at something else, maybe something with the computers, even if I don't understand them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not like the fast one, but it's in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Yusuf actually sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take him up on a job with me on a Saturday, show him what it's like. Then in the van on the way home I'd say, son, I love this work, but I'm not sure it'll be here for you. That would be hard to say, because it's what my father and I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your own work with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know some people would go off and learn something new, but that's not me. I'd do roofs till they stop paying me for roofs, and then I'd think about it.

S3.say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it, though I'd listen more when younger workers talk about it. Five years is close enough that people on the estate would be talking.
S3.think: Privately he worries most that his son would be eighteen and choosing a trade just as AGI lands. With their savings he thinks he'd get through himself, but wouldn't want his son starting on roofs then.
S3.do: Keeps working as normal and saves a bit more each month. Plans to tell his son, in a couple of years, to look at a different line of work instead of roofing.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with the worry sitting in the back of his mind.
S3.quote: Son, I love this work, but I'm not sure it'll be here for you.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Umar's concern moves almost entirely to his son's choice of trade. He's firm that he won't retrain himself and will work until roofs stop paying. The imagined talk in the van home was the most moving moment of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's a long time, a lot can happen. Probably shrug. I've seen plenty of ten-year predictions come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is fine for me. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage nearly done, the rent from the little house coming in. I'd have done my time on the roofs, and my knees would probably thank the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep paying a bit extra on the mortgage so it's finished early. And steer the kids towards something that'll last, though I couldn't tell you what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sad for the trade, but calm for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mornings, up high, seeing the estate wake up. And Pete. We've driven to work together for sixteen years and we've talked about everything in that van, his divorce, my dad dying, the football. I don't know what you replace that with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your mind and make you do something different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the firm buy one of these machines and it actually did a roof, a proper one with a valley, then I'd sit up. Until then, I'm a roofer. I'll leave the planning to people who like planning.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, and probably shrug. He's seen plenty of ten-year predictions come and go.
S4.think: Privately ten years is fine for him: at fifty-three the mortgage would be nearly done and rent from the small house would still come in. He'd have done his time on roofs, and his knees would thank the robots.
S4.do: Keeps working as he is and pays a little extra on the mortgage to finish it early. Tries to steer his children toward work that will last, though he doesn't know what that is.
S4.feel: Calm for his family, a little sad for the trade.
S4.quote: I'd have done my time on the roofs, and my knees would probably thank the robots.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lines up neatly with Umar's finances, so he relaxes. What he'd miss is less the work than the companionship, especially sixteen years of van rides with Pete. Only seeing a machine do a real roof with a valley would change his plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for the money so much, we've been careful, but because there'd be no time for Yusuf. What would help, I don't really know, I'm not a politics man. Maybe if the firms kept people on, even part-time, while the robots came in, so a man isn't just sent home after sixteen years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who fixes the robots when they break, up on a roof in January. That might be a job for someone. Not me, I'll be honest, but maybe for Yusuf, if he's got the head for it.

headlineQuote: Maybe who fixes the robots when they break, up on a roof in January. That might be a job for someone.
portrait: Umar is a 43-year-old roof carpenter who has spent sixteen years with the same family builder, riding to work every morning with his foreman and neighbour, Pete. He never uses AI, likes his routine and keeps a solid cushion of savings plus rent from a small house he owns with his brother. He shrugs at the plateau and steady pictures and publicly doubts fast AGI, though he quietly starts cutting back and worrying about his son, who wants to follow him into roofing. With five or ten years he keeps working and saving, and his main change is steering the children toward other work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly because there would be no time for his son, who wants to follow him into roofing.
whatWouldHelp: He isn't sure, but thinks firms keeping people on, even part-time, while robots come in would help, so long-serving workers aren't simply sent home.
